metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of choices that are consistent with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. For each trial, it identifies the first discriminating cue (in order of descending validity) and checks if the subject chose the option favored by that cue. Because the experimental design intentionally pits TTB against WADD on 80% of the trials (where the highest-validity discriminating cue favors one option but the sum of all lower-validity cues favors the other), data simulated under TTB will yield a score close to 1.0 (subject to noise), while data simulated under WADD will yield a score well below 0.5. This provides a massive, reliable separation between the two theories.

This metric isolates 'compensatory' trials where the Take The Best (TTB) model and the Weighted Additive (WADD) model make opposing predictions. TTB strictly follows the single highest discriminating cue, whereas WADD integrates all cues, allowing lower-validity cues to compensate. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with TTB specifically on these conflicting trials, we can cleanly separate the two theories. TTB will produce a score near 1.0, while WADD will produce a score considerably lower (often near 0.0, depending on the exact subjective feature weights).

By taking advantage of four specific trials, we can completely control for Tallying while isolating WADD's effect. Under Tallying, Trials 1, 5, 7, and 8 all have an exact feature count difference of +1 in favor of Option A. Therefore, Tallying predicts identical choice probabilities for Option A across all four trials, meaning the difference between the average choice probability of (Trial 5 + Trial 7) and (Trial 1 + Trial 8) will be precisely 0 in expectation, with low variance due to averaging. Under WADD, Option A is strongly favored in Trials 5 and 7 (average WADD score difference of +0.625) but neutral/disfavored in Trials 1 and 8 (average WADD score difference of -0.05). Thus, WADD predicts a substantially positive difference, robustly discriminating the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive (WADD) model on the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 6). On these trials, one option has fewer features but they are the highest validity ones (features 1 and 2), while the other option has more features but they are lower validity (features 3, 4, 5). The WADD model strongly prefers the option with the high-validity features, whereas the Tallying model prefers the option with the greater number of features. Consequently, WADD will score highly on this metric, while Tallying will score poorly (below 0.5, depending on noise levels).

This metric isolates 'conflict' trials where the Tallying heuristic and the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic make strictly opposing predictions. It computes the proportion of these conflict trials where the subject's choice aligns with the TTB prediction. Data generated by the TTB theory will yield a value close to 1 (minus noise), while data generated by the Tallying theory will yield a value close to 0 (plus noise), guaranteeing a large and stable discrimination.

We focus on trials where Tallying predicts a choice for option B (the sum of positive features is strictly greater for B than for A). Due to the experimental design, on all such trials, the highest validity discriminating feature favors option A, meaning Take-The-Best predicts a choice for option A. The metric calculates the proportion of choices for option A on these specific trials. Take-The-Best will yield a high value, whereas Tallying will yield a low value.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the decision-maker chooses Option A in trials 1 and 2. In these specific trials, Option A possesses the highest-validity feature(s) but has a smaller total number of positive features compared to Option B. The Tallying theory, which simply counts the number of positive features, predicts that Option B will be chosen more frequently (proportion < 0.5). In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, which weights features by their subjective validities, is likely to favor Option A (proportion > 0.5) because the presence of the most predictive features outweighs the sheer number of less predictive features.

This metric isolates the trials where the Tallying heuristic sees a perfect tie in the number of positive features between the two options (Trials 3 and 4). Because Tallying only counts features and ignores their validities, it is forced to guess on these trials, predicting exactly a 50% chance of choosing either option regardless of its noise or lapse parameters. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model evaluates the subjective validities of the features. On both Trial 3 and Trial 4, Option A possesses strictly higher-validity features than Option B. Therefore, WADD systematically prefers Option A, yielding a choice proportion significantly above 50%. By measuring the proportion of choices for Option A strictly on these Tallying-tie trials, we establish a robust, parameter-free baseline of 0.5 for Tallying, allowing WADD's validity-weighting mechanism to cleanly and significantly diverge.
